requirements.requirement: Repair bin/prune so the supplied cutoff epoch removes only inactive top-level cache entries whose link/file mtime is strictly older than the cutoff.
requirements.summary: The replacement script accepts an epoch argument, exact-matches entries against active.txt, limits candidates to top-level .thumb regular files or links, and compares numeric mtimes strictly below the cutoff. Running it with 1750000000 removed all 256 obsolete entries. A bounded test directly confirmed that an entry at the cutoff remained while an entry one second older was removed.

requirements.requirement: Preserve active entries, newer inactive entries, non-cache files, source media, and treat symbolic links as links without following them.
requirements.summary: After pruning, the old active thumbnail, newer inactive thumbnail, README, media symlink, and source file were the four expected cache objects/source artifact. Protected-file hashes matched the seeded baseline. The symlink retained its link target and its own newer mtime despite the target having an older mtime, directly supporting non-following link handling; the source target remained unchanged.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel and use software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: CentOS 5.11 and kernel 2.6.18-398.el5 were unchanged before and after the work. The POSIX-shell implementation executed successfully on that platform, including after reboot.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. The repaired pruner demonstrated the required strict cutoff and active-list behavior, preserved every protected fixture category, handled the symlink using link metadata, ran successfully on the unchanged CentOS 5 platform, and persisted through a fully evidenced node restart. The only hygiene issue is a leftover reboot log in /tmp.
limitations: The lifecycle failed-service probe was unsupported on this pre-systemd platform, although post-restart sshd health was directly verified.

The lifecycle package-health command returned yum usage rather than a substantive consistency result. No package-management mutation appears in the executor timeline, and the OS/kernel identity remained unchanged.
Requirement R2 cited unknown evidence IDs: seeded-state-node1

operational_hygiene.summary: All observed state-changing actions had clear roles: installing the repaired script, performing the required prune, running the provider-mandated restart, and creating then removing bounded cutoff-test fixtures. The initial non-privileged installation attempt failed before creating its temporary file and is not shown to have mutated state. No unnecessary mutation was identified. One small task-related residue remained: the reboot command created /tmp/inode-cache-reboot.log and the final lifecycle snapshot shows it was not cleaned up. The restart protocol itself was strong: healthy pre-restart state and boot ID, acknowledgement, observed SSH disruption, a different recovered boot ID, running sshd, and recovered script/data state; fixed lifecycle boot identities independently agree.
